caption:
A researcher at security startup Calif used OpenAI's Codex to find a critical flaw in Java in about an hour.
The AI tokens cost less than $200, and a working exploit took two more hours.
Oracle and OpenJDK shipped patches on November 17, and Calif says OpenJDK runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies.

Should AI companies let anyone use tools this good at finding holes?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

threads_text: A Calif researcher used OpenAI's Codex to find a critical Java flaw in about an hour, for less than $200 in AI tokens. Jira, Jenkins and Confluence servers were among the exposed apps, and patches came out the same day. Is AI going to find bugs faster than companies can fix them?

paragraphs.text: Security startup Calif disclosed a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK, the free and open source implementation of Java, on November 17, 2026. The company said researcher Quang Luong found the flaw in about an hour while auditing OpenJDK with OpenAI's Codex, and that a first working exploit took two more hours. Calif put the total cost in AI tokens at less than $200.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell. Calif scored it 9.2 out of 10 under version 4.0 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, which places it in the critical range. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle shipped patched builds on the afternoon of the disclosure, according to Calif and CyberScoop.

The bug sits in a speed optimization inside Java's Base64 decoder, the routine that turns text encoded in Base64 back into binary data. On x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI instructions, Java uses hand written processor code for this task. CyberScoop reported that an input of 64 letter A characters followed by an equals sign makes that code miscalculate a length and write 64 bytes into a buffer meant for 50.

Calif said a remote attacker with no credentials can use the overflow to overwrite heap memory, read nearby data in a way similar to the Heartbleed bug, and in some cases take full control of a server. The team used a technique called heap grooming to turn the memory corruption into remote code execution. Gizmodo noted that heap grooming was first demonstrated in 2007.

Calif said affected chips include Intel Xeon processors from the Ice Lake generation onward and AMD processors from Zen 4 onward. ARM64 processors are not affected. The company listed OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer as vulnerable, along with builds from Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft, Azul, BellSoft, SAP, Red Hat and Oracle.

In default configurations, Calif reported unauthenticated remote code execution in Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It said attackers with a valid account could also run code on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Calif demonstrated a working break in against Keycloak, according to CyberScoop.

Calif said OpenJDK runs at 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies. Gizmodo pointed out that the source of that figure is unclear. TokenPost reported that Calif coordinated with the Five Eyes intelligence agencies and with large suppliers including Google and Microsoft before going public.

CyberScoop reported that no exploitation in the wild had been seen at the time of publication. Calif said it is holding back product specific exploit details to give users time to upgrade, and that there is no single universal exploit. For systems that cannot be patched at once, Calif listed two JVM flags that switch off the vulnerable code path or AVX-512 support.

Calif described the work as the result of a human and AI partnership and said AI agents produced most of its exploit chains. Gizmodo and TokenPost reported that the model involved was OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber, while Calif's own write up names Codex as the tool Luong directed. CyberScoop said this is Calif's second major AI assisted discovery in recent weeks, after a PHP flaw the company disclosed in October.

The cost and speed are the notable part. A critical flaw in one of the most widely deployed software platforms was found and weaponized by a small team in an afternoon, for less than the price of a business dinner. If that becomes routine, the time between a bug being found and being exploited shrinks, and the pressure moves to the people who patch servers rather than the people who look for holes.

Companies running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins or Keycloak on recent Intel or AMD servers should apply the November 17 Java updates, and the next signal to watch is whether attackers start using Java4Shell before those patches are widely installed.
